lead: Two metal plates with an insulator between them store charge when a voltage is applied. The capacitance depends on plate area, plate gap and the dielectric between them. A capacitive transducer makes one of these three quantities follow the measurand, so capacitance becomes a measure of displacement, pressure, level or humidity. The change is small, often less than a picofarad, so a signal-conditioning circuit must convert it into a usable voltage. These transducers load the object very little, resolve nanometre motion, and are cheap to make, which is why they sit inside phones, touch panels, pressure gauges and microphones.
prereq: You need: electrostatics, namely C = Q/V and the parallel-plate capacitor, plus resolution and linearity from the static characteristics of sensors.

sections.h3: The parallel-plate capacitor as a sensor

blocks.text: Capacitance is the charge stored per volt, C = Q/V, measured in farads (F). For two parallel plates the value is fixed by geometry and material.

blocks.where: C is capacitance in farads (F); ε₀ is the permittivity of free space = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² F/m; εr is the relative permittivity of the material between the plates (1.0006 for air, about 2.1 for PTFE, about 80 for water); A is the overlapping plate area in square metres (m²); d is the plate gap in metres (m).

blocks.text: A transducer moves exactly one of d, A or εr with the measurand and holds the other two fixed. The capacitance then carries the reading.

The capacitance itself is small: a plate of 100 mm² at a 0.5 mm gap gives only about 1.8 pF, and the changes to be measured are fractions of that. The circuit therefore works in picofarads. The plates can be light and stiff, so the sensor barely loads the object and can resolve nanometre motion. The same smallness is the weakness — a few picofarads of cable capacitance is as large as the signal.

items: High resolution and low force on the object.
C ∝ 1/d when the gap moves, so the response is nonlinear.
Stray capacitance, cable length and temperature set the accuracy limit.

sections.h3: The three types and their construction

items: Variable gap: a diaphragm or moving plate changes d. Used for pressure and sound (see 3.7) and for small displacements. Because C ∝ 1/d, the movement is kept to a small fraction of d so the curve stays near linear.
Variable area: one plate slides over the other, so A changes at fixed d. C ∝ A, so the output is linear in displacement, and shaped plates give a chosen law for angular sensing.

Variable dielectric: a material of different εr moves into the gap. Used for liquid level (a vertical rod dipped in the liquid), sheet thickness, humidity (a polymer film whose εr follows moisture) and touch (a finger changes the field).

blocks.text: A differential (three-plate) sensor puts a moving plate midway between two fixed plates, each gap d. Moving it by x gives C₁ = ε₀A/(d − x) and C₂ = ε₀A/(d + x). In a transformer-ratio bridge the output is (Vs/2)(C₁ − C₂)/(C₁ + C₂) = (Vs/2)·x/d: exactly linear, with temperature and dielectric changes common to both halves cancelling (worked example 2).

In medicine: capacitive pressure sensors in ventilators and anaesthesia machines, capacitive humidity sensors in incubators and breathing-gas humidifiers, capacitive MEMS accelerometers in activity and fall monitors, and capacitive electrodes that pick up the ECG through clothing.

Construction is two plates inside a metal case. One plate is often a thin diaphragm clamped over a back plate, with a gap of 0.05 mm to 0.5 mm filled with air, oil or a solid dielectric. A guard ring surrounds the measuring plate: a metal ring held at the same potential by a guard drive. Field lines that would leave the plate edge and reach the case end on the guard instead, so they are not counted in the measurement. The case is grounded and the cable is shielded, with the shield driven at guard potential.

sections.h3: Signal conditioning: from picofarads to volts

items: Excite with an AC carrier, typically 1 kHz to 100 kHz at a few volts. AC avoids charge build-up and lets a bridge work.
Convert C to voltage: an AC bridge with the sensor as one arm, or a capacitance-to-voltage converter (charge amplifier, switched-capacitor or sigma-delta type) giving V ∝ C.
Amplify the bridge output with a high-input-impedance amplifier; the bridge is balanced at the zero position, so its output is near zero there and grows with the change.
Demodulate with a phase-sensitive detector, so the output is DC and keeps the sign of the capacitance change.
Filter out carrier ripple, then linearise, because a gap sensor follows 1/d and needs correction.
Drive the guard and the cable shield from a buffer at signal potential, so stray capacitance to the shield draws no current from the measuring node.

blocks.text: Keep the input cable short and the node guarded. Every extra picofarad at the input adds to C and reads as a gap error. Keep the electronics at stable temperature, because εr and plate size drift with heat.

examples.question: A parallel-plate capacitive displacement sensor has plate area A = 100 mm², air gap d = 0.50 mm, and air with εr = 1. Take ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² F/m. (a) Find C. (b) The gap falls to 0.40 mm; find the new C and the percentage change in C. (c) Why is the percentage change in C larger than the percentage change in d?
steps: Convert units: A = 100 mm² = 100 × 10⁻⁶ m² = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ m². d = 0.50 mm = 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ m.
Numerator = 8.854 × 10⁻¹⁶ F·m. Divide by 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ m: C = 1.771 × 10⁻¹² F ≈ 1.77 pF.
The gap fell by 0.10/0.50 = 20 %, but C follows 1/d and the ratio 0.50/0.40 = 1.25, so C rises by 25 %. Only for very small movements does ΔC/C ≈ −Δd/d hold; at 20 % the nonlinearity shows.
examples.answer: C = 1.77 pF at a 0.50 mm gap, rising to 2.21 pF at a 0.40 mm gap, a change of 25.0 %.

examples.question: A three-plate differential sensor has A = 100 mm² and d = 0.50 mm of air on each side, in a transformer-ratio bridge at 10 V rms. The centre plate moves 0.05 mm towards plate 1. Find C₁, C₂ and the output, and compare with the single-gap sensor of worked example 1.
steps: Output = (10/2) × 0.100 = 0.500 V rms; a 0.05 mm move the other way gives 0.500 V rms in antiphase.
Single gap: 1.771 pF → 1.968 pF is +11.1 % for a 10 % gap change, and −0.05 mm gives −9.1 %: unequal, so non-linear.
examples.answer: C₁ = 1.968 pF, C₂ = 1.610 pF, output 0.500 V rms, exactly proportional to x; the single gap gives +11.1 % and −9.1 %.

traps: Treating C as linear in gap. C ∝ 1/d, so a 20 % fall in gap gives a 25 % rise in C, and the error grows as the movement becomes a larger share of d.

Ignoring stray capacitance. Cable and amplifier input add picofarads in parallel with a sensor that may itself be only 2 pF, so the offset and its drift can exceed the signal. Guard and shield the input node.

Using the wrong type for the job: gap for pressure, sound and very small displacements, area for larger displacements, dielectric for level, thickness and humidity. A gap sensor used for level gives the wrong law.
Unit slips: 1 mm² = 10⁻⁶ m² and 1 mm = 10⁻³ m, so a 0.5 mm gap is 5 × 10⁻⁴ m, not 5 × 10⁻³ m. A wrong power of ten here moves the answer by ten.

quiz.q: Write the parallel-plate capacitance formula and give the unit of each symbol.
quiz.a: C = ε₀εrA/d, with C in F, ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² F/m, εr dimensionless, A in m², d in m.

quiz.q: Name the three types of capacitive transducer by the quantity that changes.
quiz.a: Variable gap (d changes), variable area (A changes), variable dielectric (εr changes).

quiz.q: Why is a variable-gap sensor nonlinear while a variable-area sensor is linear?
quiz.a: C ∝ 1/d, so equal steps of gap give unequal steps of capacitance. C ∝ A, so equal steps of area give equal steps of capacitance when d and εr are fixed.

quiz.q: A capacitive sensor reads 200 pF at d = 1.0 mm. The gap opens to 1.2 mm with A and εr fixed. Find C and the percentage change.
A 1.8 pF sensor is joined by a cable that adds 30 pF. Explain the error and how a driven shield removes it.
quiz.a: The cable capacitance is in parallel, so the input sees about 31.8 pF and the signal is a tiny part of a large, drifting offset, which destroys resolution. With a driven shield the shield is held at the same potential as the centre conductor, no current flows through the cable capacitance, and the input node sees only the sensor.

quiz.q: Why is AC excitation preferred over DC for a capacitive transducer?
quiz.a: A capacitor passes no steady current: with DC the plates charge once and then nothing flows, so there is no continuous signal, only a decaying transient. AC gives a steady impedance 1/(ωC) that a bridge can measure, and moves the signal away from DC offsets and low-frequency noise.

beyond: Not for the exam. Capacitive sensing has moved into MEMS: silicon microphones, accelerometers and pressure dies etch a diaphragm a few micrometres from a back plate and read the change with an on-chip capacitance-to-digital converter. Touch panels use the same physics in two modes, self-capacitance for a single finger and mutual capacitance for multi-touch. Research goes into active guarding, ratiometric sigma-delta front ends, and flexible capacitive skins for robots and wearable health patches. Useful search terms: capacitance-to-digital converter, driven shield, guarded capacitive sensor, mutual-capacitance touch.
